claim: The cerebellum is composed of a cortex and several nuclei.
source: The cerebellum, a crucial center for motor coordination, is composed of a cortex and several nuclei.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a basic anatomical fact about the cerebellum.

claim: The main mode of interaction between cerebellar cortex and nuclei is considered to be formed by the inhibitory control of the nuclei by cortical Purkinje neurons.
source: The main mode of interaction between these two parts is considered to be formed by the inhibitory control of the nuclei by cortical Purkinje neurons.
evidence: This represents the established view in the field that is being amended by the current study.

claim: Inhibitory GABA-glycinergic neurons of the cerebellar nuclei project profusely into the cerebellar cortex.
source: We now amend this view by showing that inhibitory GABA-glycinergic neurons of the cerebellar nuclei (CN) project profusely into the cerebellar cortex, where they make synaptic contacts on a GABAergic subpopulation of cerebellar Golgi cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by anatomical data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Inhibitory nucleo-cortical neurons make synaptic contacts on a GABAergic subpopulation of cerebellar Golgi cells.
source: We now amend this view by showing that inhibitory GABA-glycinergic neurons of the cerebellar nuclei (CN) project profusely into the cerebellar cortex, where they make synaptic contacts on a GABAergic subpopulation of cerebellar Golgi cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical and electrophysiological data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Spontaneously firing Golgi cells are inhibited by optogenetic activation of the inhibitory nucleo-cortical fibers both in vitro and in vivo.
source: These spontaneously firing Golgi cells are inhibited by optogenetic activation of the inhibitory nucleo-cortical fibers both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: The cerebellar nuclei may contribute to the functional recruitment of the cerebellar cortex by decreasing Golgi cell inhibition onto granule cells.
source: Our data suggest that the CN may contribute to the functional recruitment of the cerebellar cortex by decreasing Golgi cell inhibition onto granule cells.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on the experimental findings and known circuit properties.

claim: The cerebellum plays a key role in the fine temporal control of posture and movements as well as in cognitive processes.
source: The cerebellum plays a key role in the fine temporal control of posture and movements as well as in cognitive processes (Ito, 1993; Leiner et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Current cerebellar theories mainly discuss cerebellar computation from the point of view of its cortical circuitry.
source: Current cerebellar theories (Apps and Garwicz, 2005; Jacobson et al., 2008; Dean and Porrill, 2011) mainly discuss cerebellar computation from the point of view of its cortical circuitry, where both pre-cerebellar mossy fibers (MFs) and inferior olive (IO)-originating climbing fibers (CFs) modulate Purkinje neuron (PN) spiking.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work in the field.

claim: Sensory-motor signal processing in the cerebellar nuclei has received less attention than cortical processing.
source: Sensory-motor signal processing in the main cerebellar output structure, the cerebellar nuclei (CN), has received less attention.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field that provides context for the study.

claim: Modulation of spike frequency and timing in the CN projection neurons is considered to be mostly determined by the massive inhibitory cortico-nuclear projection of PNs.
source: Modulation of spike frequency and timing in the CN projection neurons is considered to be mostly determined by the massive inhibitory cortico-nuclear projection of PNs (Chan-Palay, 1977; De Zeeuw and Berrebi, 1995; Gauck and Jaeger, 2000; Telgkamp and Raman, 2002; Pedroarena and Schwarz, 2003; Telgkamp et al., 2004; Person and Raman, 2012; Najac and Raman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Certain aspects of cerebellar function persist even when the cerebellar cortex is selectively inactivated or damaged.
source: However, certain aspects of cerebellar function persist even when the cerebellar cortex is selectively inactivated or damaged (Thompson and Steinmetz, 2009; Aoki et al., 2014; Clopath et al., 2014; Longley and Yeo, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The cerebellar cortex and the CN interact through the nucleo-olivary circuit.
source: Currently, the cerebellar cortex and the CN are known to interact through two circuits. The best known is the nucleo-olivary (NO) circuit (Apps and Garwicz, 2005; Apps and Hawkes, 2009; Chaumont et al., 2013), where the small GABAergic CN cells, subject to PN inhibition (Najac and Raman, 2015), project to the contralateral IO (Fredette and Mugnaini, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical and functional studies.

claim: The nucleo-olivary pathway regulates olivary activity.
source: This pathway regulates olivary activity (Chen et al., 2010; Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012; Chaumont et al., 2013; Lefler et al., 2014) and thereby complex spike activity in the PNs and cerebellar cortical plasticity (Hansel and Linden, 2000; Coesmans et al., 2004; Bengtsson and Hesslow, 2006; Medina and Lisberger, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to functional studies.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons of the CN send axonal collaterals to the cerebellar granule cell layer.
source: A less-known nucleo-cortical circuit is formed by the glutamatergic neurons of the CN which, in addition to projecting to various premotor and associative regions of the brain (Tsukahara and Bando, 1970; Asanuma et al., 1980; Angaut et al., 1985; Sultan et al., 2012; Ruigrok and Teune, 2014), send axonal collaterals to the cerebellar granule cell layer (GrCL; Houck and Person, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Glutamatergic nucleo-cortical collateral fibers form MF-like terminals contacting granule cell and Golgi cell dendrites.
source: These collateral fibers form MF-like terminals contacting granule cell (GrC) and Golgi cell dendrites (see also Tolbert et al., 1976, 1977, 1978; Hámori et al., 1980; Payne, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ultrastructural studies.

claim: The functional significance of the excitatory nucleo-cortical pathway is likely related to efference copying of motor commands to the cerebellar cortex.
source: The functional significance of this excitatory nucleo-cortical (eNC) pathway, loosely following the modular arrangement of the cerebellum (Dietrichs and Walberg, 1979; Gould, 1979; Haines and Pearson, 1979; Tolbert and Bantli, 1979; Buisseret-Delmas, 1988; Provini et al., 1998; Ruigrok, 2010 ; reviewed by Houck and Person, 2013), is likely related to efference copying of motor commands to the cerebellar cortex (Sommer and Wurtz, 2008; Houck and Person, 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: GABAergic neurons have been shown to be labeled in the CN by retrograde tracing from the cerebellar cortex.
source: GABAergic neurons have been shown to be labeled in the CN by retrograde tracing from the cerebellar cortex (Batini et al., 1989), and nucleo-cortical terminals with non-glutamatergic ultrastructural features have been found to contact putative Golgi cell dendrites (Tolbert et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical tracing studies.

claim: GlyT2-expressing CN neurons extend axons toward the cerebellar cortex.
source: More recently, it was demonstrated that GlyT2-expressing CN neurons extend axons toward the cerebellar cortex (Uusisaari and Knöpfel, 2010), suggesting that the iNC pathway might be identifiable by its glycinergic phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous anatomical study.

claim: The postsynaptic targets and functional organization of the iNC pathway remain unknown.
source: While the iNC projection is likely to have significant impact on cerebellar computation, its postsynaptic targets and its functional organization remain unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Specific viral targeting of GABAergic and glycinergic neurons in the CN was employed using GAD-cre and GlyT2-cre transgenic mouse lines.
source: To establish the existence and prevalence of an inhibitory connection between the CN and the cerebellar cortex, we employed specific viral targeting of GABAergic and glycinergic neurons in the CN of GAD-cre and GlyT2-cre transgenic mouse lines, respectively (Taniguchi et al., 2011; Husson et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: GABA-glycinergic CN neurons form an extensive plexus of iNC axons.
source: We found that the GABA-glycinergic CN neurons form an extensive plexus of iNC axons, which contact Golgi cells in the cerebellar granular and molecular layers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by anatomical data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: iNC axons contact Golgi cells in the cerebellar granular and molecular layers.
source: We found that the GABA-glycinergic CN neurons form an extensive plexus of iNC axons, which contact Golgi cells in the cerebellar granular and molecular layers.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Specific optogenetic activation of the iNC axons inhibited spikes in a distinct subpopulation of Golgi cells.
source: Specific optogenetic activation of the iNC axons inhibited spikes in a distinct subpopulation of Golgi cells, characterized by their spontaneous firing, high neurogranin immunoreactivity, and negligible GlyT2 expression.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data in Figures 3, 4, and 6, and immunohistochemical data in Figure 5.

claim: The iNC-targeted Golgi cells are characterized by spontaneous firing, high neurogranin immunoreactivity, and negligible GlyT2 expression.
source: Specific optogenetic activation of the iNC axons inhibited spikes in a distinct subpopulation of Golgi cells, characterized by their spontaneous firing, high neurogranin immunoreactivity, and negligible GlyT2 expression.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4 and immunohistochemical data in Figure 5.

claim: The functional significance of the iNC pathway is likely to be amplified by the high divergence of Golgi cells.
source: As the functional significance of the iNC pathway is likely to be amplified by the high divergence of Golgi cells, which target thousands of GrCs (Hámori and Somogyi, 1983; Jakab and Hamori, 1988; Andersen et al., 1992; Korbo et al., 1993), as well as the remarkable mediolateral extent of the iNC axons, the CN might play a key role in the regulation of the information flow through the GrCL.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on known circuit properties and the current findings.

claim: Golgi cells target thousands of granule cells.
source: As the functional significance of the iNC pathway is likely to be amplified by the high divergence of Golgi cells, which target thousands of GrCs (Hámori and Somogyi, 1983; Jakab and Hamori, 1988; Andersen et al., 1992; Korbo et al., 1993), as well as the remarkable mediolateral extent of the iNC axons, the CN might play a key role in the regulation of the information flow through the GrCL.
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The CN might play a key role in the regulation of the information flow through the GrCL.
source: As the functional significance of the iNC pathway is likely to be amplified by the high divergence of Golgi cells, which target thousands of GrCs (Hámori and Somogyi, 1983; Jakab and Hamori, 1988; Andersen et al., 1992; Korbo et al., 1993), as well as the remarkable mediolateral extent of the iNC axons, the CN might play a key role in the regulation of the information flow through the GrCL.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on the anatomical and physiological findings.

claim: Floxed adeno-associated virus injection in the CN of GAD-cre mice resulted in expression of mCherry in a subset of CN neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 1A1,B1, these procedures resulted in the expression of the fluorophores (mCherry in GAD-cre and YFP in GlyT2-cre mice) in a subset of CN neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the confocal images in Figure 1A1.

claim: Floxed adeno-associated virus injection in the CN of GlyT2-cre mice resulted in expression of YFP in a subset of CN neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 1A1,B1, these procedures resulted in the expression of the fluorophores (mCherry in GAD-cre and YFP in GlyT2-cre mice) in a subset of CN neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the confocal images in Figure 1B1.

claim: In GAD-cre mice, labeled neurons displayed a wide range of sizes and shapes, including both globular and multipolar morphologies.
source: In the GAD-cre mice, the labeled neurons displayed a wide range of sizes and shapes, including both globular and multipolar morphologies (Figure 1A2, arrow and arrowhead, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal images in Figure 1A2.

claim: In GlyT2-cre mice, labeled neurons were predominantly large and multipolar, often with a thick principal dendrite.
source: In contrast, in GlyT2-cre mice, the labeled neurons were predominantly large (Figure 1B2, arrowhead) and multipolar, often with a thick principal dendrite (Figure 1B2, arrows).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal images in Figure 1B2.

claim: The size distribution in GAD-cre CN was best fitted with a two-component Gaussian model with peaks at 11.9 µm and 16.2 µm.
source: The size distribution in GAD-cre CN was best fitted with a two-component Gaussian model (Figure 1D, red bars and line; Gaussian peaks at 11.9 µm and 16.2 µm; R-square 0.97, n = 650 cells in 6 animals), suggesting it is composed of two separate populations.
evidence: This is shown by the histogram and fit in Figure 1D.

claim: The GAD-cre CN neuron size distribution suggests it is composed of two separate populations.
source: The size distribution in GAD-cre CN was best fitted with a two-component Gaussian model (Figure 1D, red bars and line; Gaussian peaks at 11.9 µm and 16.2 µm; R-square 0.97, n = 650 cells in 6 animals), suggesting it is composed of two separate populations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The optimal fit to the size distribution of GlyT2-cre neurons was obtained with a single-component Gaussian model with peak at 16.6 µm.
source: In contrast, the optimal fit to the size distribution of GlyT2-cre neurons was obtained with a single-component Gaussian model (Figure 1D, yellow bars and line; peak at 16.6 µm, R-square = 0.83, n = 118 cells in 4 animals; KS-test GAD vs GlyT2, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is shown by the histogram and fit in Figure 1D.

claim: The size distributions of GAD-cre and GlyT2-cre CN neurons are significantly different.
source: In contrast, the optimal fit to the size distribution of GlyT2-cre neurons was obtained with a single-component Gaussian model (Figure 1D, yellow bars and line; peak at 16.6 µm, R-square = 0.83, n = 118 cells in 4 animals; KS-test GAD vs GlyT2, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the KS-test result reported in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The peak of the GlyT2-cre neuron size distribution matched well with the right-most peak in the GAD-cre distribution.
source: The peak of this GlyT2-fit matched well with the right-most peak in the GAD-cre distribution (GAD-cre, second peak confidence interval, 13.6–18.8 µm; GlyT2-cre confidence interval, 16.0–17.1 µm).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the confidence intervals in Figure 1D.

claim: The mixed GABA-glycinergic neurons form a separate population from the purely GABAergic NO neurons.
source: Thus, we conclude that the mixed GABA-glycinergic neurons form a separate population from the purely GABAergic NO neurons that are not transfected in adult GlyT2-cre animals (Husson et al., 2014).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the size distribution analysis in Figure 1D and comparison with NO neurons.

claim: Purely GABAergic NO neurons are not transfected in adult GlyT2-cre animals.
source: Thus, we conclude that the mixed GABA-glycinergic neurons form a separate population from the purely GABAergic NO neurons that are not transfected in adult GlyT2-cre animals (Husson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Glycinergic CN neurons receive functional inputs from PN axons.
source: These glycinergic neurons, like all other CN neurons, receive functional inputs from PN axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as previously suggested by immunohistochemical and optogenetic studies (De Zeeuw and Berrebi, 1995; Teune et al., 1998).
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: Axons of the large multipolar GAD and GlyT2-positive neurons projected across the white matter surrounding the CN and into the cerebellar cortex.
source: In contrast to the NO axons, which leave the CN towards the brainstem, we found that axons of the large multipolar GAD and GlyT2-positive neurons projected across the white matter surrounding the CN and into the cerebellar cortex (as shown in Figure 1E1,2 for the GAD-cre and GlyT2-cre cerebella, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal images in Figure 1E1,2.

claim: In the vermis, the nucleo-cortical projections regularly crossed the midline and extended into the contralateral cortex.
source: In the vermis, the projections regularly crossed the midline and extended into the contralateral cortex, but otherwise the projection was predominantly ipsilateral.
evidence: This is an anatomical observation from the viral tracing experiments.

claim: The nucleo-cortical projection was predominantly ipsilateral.
source: In the vermis, the projections regularly crossed the midline and extended into the contralateral cortex, but otherwise the projection was predominantly ipsilateral.
evidence: This is an anatomical observation from the viral tracing experiments.

claim: The divergence of nucleo-cortical axons in the cortex varied depending on the extent and localization of viral transfection, coarsely following the known cerebellar modules.
source: The divergence of nucleo-cortical axons in the cortex varied depending on the extent and localization of viral transfection, coarsely following the known cerebellar modules (Apps and Garwicz, 2005; Pijpers et al., 2005; Apps and Hawkes, 2009).
evidence: This is an observation from the anatomical tracing experiments supported by citations to modular organization.

claim: Lateral CN injections labeled axons in the lateral and intermediate hemispheres and the flocculi.
source: Lateral CN injections labeled axons in the lateral and intermediate hemispheres and the flocculi (Figure 1F1), whereas medial CN injections yielded labeled axons predominantly in the vermal cerebellum (Figure 1F2).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal images in Figure 1F1.

claim: Medial CN injections yielded labeled axons predominantly in the vermal cerebellum.
source: Lateral CN injections labeled axons in the lateral and intermediate hemispheres and the flocculi (Figure 1F1), whereas medial CN injections yielded labeled axons predominantly in the vermal cerebellum (Figure 1F2).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal images in Figure 1F2.

claim: Individual nucleo-cortical axons could be seen to travel long distances in the medio-lateral direction (up to several millimeters) forming boutons within the GrCL.
source: Surprisingly, individual nucleo-cortical axons could be seen to travel long distances in the medio-lateral direction (up to several millimeters; see inset in Figure 1F2) forming boutons within the GrCL.
evidence: This is shown in the inset of Figure 1F2.

claim: The nucleo-cortical axons formed dense meshes in the GrCL.
source: The nucleo-cortical axons formed dense meshes in the GrCL (Figure 2A1,B1).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal images in Figure 2A1,B1.

claim: The iNC axons formed large swellings in the granular cell layer and molecular layer.
source: As seen in high-magnification images (Figure 2A2,B2), the axons formed large swellings that were also seen in the molecular layer (ML; Figure 2A3,B3).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal images in Figure 2A2,B2,A3,B3.

claim: The axons in the GAD-cre and GlyT2-cre lines were remarkably similar in their appearance.
source: The axons in the two cre lines were remarkably similar in their appearance, even though the swellings labeled with mCherry in the GAD-cre line appeared nearly identical to the varicosities labeled by YFP in the GlyT2-cre line (Figure 2A2,B2,C1; cross-sectional areas in GAD-cre, red bars, 2.1 ± 0.9 µm2, n = 400 varicosities; in GlyT2-cre, yellow bars, 1.87 ± 0.9 µm2, n = 415 varicosities; KS-test, p = 0.013).
evidence: This is shown by the morphological comparison in Figure 2 and quantitative analysis in Figure 2C1.

claim: The cross-sectional areas of axonal swellings in GAD-cre mice were 2.1 ± 0.9 µm2.
source: The axons in the two cre lines were remarkably similar in their appearance, even though the swellings labeled with mCherry in the GAD-cre line appeared nearly identical to the varicosities labeled by YFP in the GlyT2-cre line (Figure 2A2,B2,C1; cross-sectional areas in GAD-cre, red bars, 2.1 ± 0.9 µm2, n = 400 varicosities; in GlyT2-cre, yellow bars, 1.87 ± 0.9 µm2, n = 415 varicosities; KS-test, p = 0.013).
evidence: This is quantified from the confocal images and shown in Figure 2C1.

claim: The cross-sectional areas of axonal swellings in GlyT2-cre mice were 1.87 ± 0.9 µm2.
source: The axons in the two cre lines were remarkably similar in their appearance, even though the swellings labeled with mCherry in the GAD-cre line appeared nearly identical to the varicosities labeled by YFP in the GlyT2-cre line (Figure 2A2,B2,C1; cross-sectional areas in GAD-cre, red bars, 2.1 ± 0.9 µm2, n = 400 varicosities; in GlyT2-cre, yellow bars, 1.87 ± 0.9 µm2, n = 415 varicosities; KS-test, p = 0.013).
evidence: This is quantified from the confocal images and shown in Figure 2C1.

claim: No large differences were evident among boutons found in the GrCL or ML.
source: Also, no large differences were evident among boutons found in the GrCL or ML (Figure 2C2; KS-test, p = 0.023).
evidence: This is shown by the comparison in Figure 2C2.

claim: The anatomical similarities imply that the axons labeled in the two transfection models represent the projections of a specific population of CN neurons with a mixed GABA-glycinergic phenotype.
source: These anatomical similarities imply that the axons labeled in the two transfection models represent the projections of a specific population of CN neurons with a mixed GABA-glycinergic phenotype (Husson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical data and supported by citation.

claim: Virtually all the nucleo-cortical fibers in the GAD-cre transfected mice were immunoreactive for GlyT2 (94.6 ± 6.2%).
source: Indeed, immunostaining revealed that virtually all the nucleo-cortical fibers in the GAD-cre transfected mice were immunoreactive for GlyT2 (Figure 2D1–2; 94.6 ± 6.2%, n = 2 animals, n = 9 stacks, n = 422 varicosities; Figure 2D), while those in GlyT2-cre cerebella were reactive for GAD65-67 (93.9 ± 5.0%, n = 3 animals, n = 7 stacks, n = 565 varicosities; Figure 2E1–2).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemical staining in Figure 2D1-2.

claim: Nucleo-cortical fibers in GlyT2-cre cerebella were reactive for GAD65-67 (93.9 ± 5.0%).
source: Indeed, immunostaining revealed that virtually all the nucleo-cortical fibers in the GAD-cre transfected mice were immunoreactive for GlyT2 (Figure 2D1–2; 94.6 ± 6.2%, n = 2 animals, n = 9 stacks, n = 422 varicosities; Figure 2D), while those in GlyT2-cre cerebella were reactive for GAD65-67 (93.9 ± 5.0%, n = 3 animals, n = 7 stacks, n = 565 varicosities; Figure 2E1–2).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemical staining in Figure 2E1-2.

claim: The immunostaining results unequivocally demonstrate the dual neurotransmitter phenotype of the nucleo-cortical projection.
source: These results unequivocally demonstrate the dual neurotransmitter phenotype of the nucleo-cortical projection.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the immunohistochemical data in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Neither rosette-like terminals nor evidence of contacts within cerebellar glomeruli was found for iNC axons.
source: Notably, neither rosette-like terminals nor evidence of contacts within cerebellar glomeruli was found.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the anatomical examination.

claim: iNC axons differ both in shape and location from the excitatory MFs and the glutamatergic nucleo-cortical fibers.
source: This indicates that they differ both in shape and location from the excitatory MFs and the glutamatergic nucleo-cortical fibers described earlier in the literature, both forming rosette-like terminals within the glomeruli (Tolbert et al., 1978; Hámori et al., 1980; Batini et al., 1992; Houck and Person, 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical observations and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Axonal swellings of iNC fibers were found apposed along the proximal dendrites and cell bodies of Golgi cells.
source: This procedure labeled Golgi cells and indeed we found axonal swellings of iNC fibers apposed along the proximal dendrites and cell bodies of Golgi cells (Figure 3A, arrows).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal image and reconstruction in Figure 3A.

claim: Inhibitory post-synaptic currents were evoked in 9 out of 38 recorded Golgi cells (23.7%) by optogenetic stimulation of iNC fibers.
source: Inhibitory post-synaptic currents (IPSCs) were evoked in 9 out of 38 recorded Golgi cells (23.7%; Figure 3C1) with a mean amplitude of 40 ± 28 pA.
evidence: This is shown by the voltage-clamp recordings in Figure 3C1.

claim: The mean amplitude of light-evoked IPSCs in Golgi cells was 40 ± 28 pA.
source: Inhibitory post-synaptic currents (IPSCs) were evoked in 9 out of 38 recorded Golgi cells (23.7%; Figure 3C1) with a mean amplitude of 40 ± 28 pA.
evidence: This is measured from the voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: The chord synaptic conductance of iNC synapses was 1.7 ± 1.2 nS.
source: Given the ionic composition of our experimental solutions, the estimated reversal potential of −74 mV with the permeabilities of bicarbonate and chloride taken into account and the holding potential of −50 mV, the chord synaptic conductance was 1.7 ± 1.2 nS and the slope conductance was 1.9 ± 1.3 nS according to the Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz (GHK) equation.
evidence: This is calculated from the voltage-clamp data using the GHK equation.

claim: The slope conductance of iNC synapses was 1.9 ± 1.3 nS.
source: Given the ionic composition of our experimental solutions, the estimated reversal potential of −74 mV with the permeabilities of bicarbonate and chloride taken into account and the holding potential of −50 mV, the chord synaptic conductance was 1.7 ± 1.2 nS and the slope conductance was 1.9 ± 1.3 nS according to the Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz (GHK) equation.
evidence: This is calculated from the voltage-clamp data using the GHK equation.

claim: The equivalent peak conductance of the iNC synapse measured in symmetrical chloride conditions would have been 8.5 ± 5.9 nS.
source: We calculated that the equivalent peak conductance of the iNC synapse measured in symmetrical chloride conditions would have been of 8.5 ± 5.9 nS.
evidence: This is calculated from the voltage-clamp data.

claim: The light-evoked IPSCs had a 10–90% rise time of 2.5 ± 1.3 ms.
source: The light-evoked IPSCs had a 10–90% rise time of 2.5 ± 1.3 ms and a bi-exponential decay (τ1 = 8.2 ± 1.9 ms, 52.3 ± 18.3%; τ2 = 34.8 ± 9.2 ms, n = 9 cells).
evidence: This is measured from the voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: The light-evoked IPSCs had a bi-exponential decay with τ1 = 8.2 ± 1.9 ms (52.3 ± 18.3%) and τ2 = 34.8 ± 9.2 ms.
source: The light-evoked IPSCs had a 10–90% rise time of 2.5 ± 1.3 ms and a bi-exponential decay (τ1 = 8.2 ± 1.9 ms, 52.3 ± 18.3%; τ2 = 34.8 ± 9.2 ms, n = 9 cells).
evidence: This is measured from the voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: Application of strychnine at 300 nM decreased the amplitude of the IPSC by 24 ± 25%.
source: Application of strychnine at a concentration selective for glycine receptors (300 nM) decreased the amplitude of the IPSC by 24 ± 25% (p = 0.039, n = 9 cells) without affecting the time course of the IPSCs (rise time: 2.4 ± 0.9 ms; decay: τ1 = 9.2 ± 3.0 ms, 52.5 ± 23.5%, τ2 = 40.6 ± 21.2 ms; p = 0.91, p = 0.65 and p = 1.00 respectively, n = 9 cells).
evidence: This is shown by the pharmacological experiments in Figure 3C1,C2.

claim: Strychnine application did not affect the time course of the IPSCs.
source: Application of strychnine at a concentration selective for glycine receptors (300 nM) decreased the amplitude of the IPSC by 24 ± 25% (p = 0.039, n = 9 cells) without affecting the time course of the IPSCs (rise time: 2.4 ± 0.9 ms; decay: τ1 = 9.2 ± 3.0 ms, 52.5 ± 23.5%, τ2 = 40.6 ± 21.2 ms; p = 0.91, p = 0.65 and p = 1.00 respectively, n = 9 cells).
evidence: This is shown by the pharmacological experiments.

claim: The results confirm the presence of a glycinergic component at the iNC-Golgi cell synapses with large variability in its magnitude (range: 0–63%).
source: These results confirm the presence of a glycinergic component at the iNC-Golgi cell synapses albeit with large variability in its magnitude (range: 0–63%; Figure 3C2, left).
evidence: This is shown by the pharmacological experiments in Figure 3C2.

claim: Subsequent application of gabazine (2 µM) almost completely blocked the IPSC response, decreasing the amplitude by 96.5 ± 2.9%.
source: Subsequent application of a GABAA-receptor antagonist (gabazine, 2 µM), almost completely blocked the response, decreasing the amplitude of the IPSC by 96.5 ± 2.9% (p = 0.0078, n = 8 cells; Figure 3C1,2).
evidence: This is shown by the pharmacological experiments in Figure 3C1,2.

claim: The pharmacological results confirm the mixed GABAergic-glycinergic nature of the iNC axons.
source: These results confirm the mixed GABAergic-glycinergic nature of the iNC axons.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the pharmacological experiments in Figure 3C.

claim: Whole-field light stimulation of the iNC axons had a significant effect on the spiking in 24 out of 86 recorded Golgi cells (27%).
source: Whole-field light stimulation of the iNC axons had a significant effect on the spiking in 24 out of 86 recorded Golgi cells (27%; Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is shown by the current-clamp recordings in Figure 3D-G.

claim: A single 5-ms light pulse elicited clear inhibitory responses in most cases, involving a hyperpolarizing post-synaptic potential (n = 12 cells; IPSP amplitude 2.1 ± 1.5 mV).
source: A single 5-ms light pulse elicited clear inhibitory responses in most of cases, involving a hyperpolarizing post-synaptic potential (n = 12 cells; IPSP amplitude 2.1 ± 1.5 mV; Figure 3D) and/or prolongation of the inter-spike interval (ISI) during which the stimulation occurred (n = 15 cells; 60 ± 30% increase; on average, 223 ± 123 ms ISI increased to 355 ± 286 ms; cells; p = 0.0001, paired t-test; Figure 3E1,E2).
evidence: This is shown by the current-clamp recordings in Figure 3D.

claim: A single 5-ms light pulse caused prolongation of the inter-spike interval (n = 15 cells; 60 ± 30% increase; on average, 223 ± 123 ms ISI increased to 355 ± 286 ms).
source: A single 5-ms light pulse elicited clear inhibitory responses in most of cases, involving a hyperpolarizing post-synaptic potential (n = 12 cells; IPSP amplitude 2.1 ± 1.5 mV; Figure 3D) and/or prolongation of the inter-spike interval (ISI) during which the stimulation occurred (n = 15 cells; 60 ± 30% increase; on average, 223 ± 123 ms ISI increased to 355 ± 286 ms; cells; p = 0.0001, paired t-test; Figure 3E1,E2).
evidence: This is shown by the current-clamp recordings in Figure 3E1,E2.

claim: Inhibition of spiking was more pronounced when iNC fibers were activated with a train of 4–5 light pulses at 50 Hz, eliciting a longer spike delay (71 ± 44% increase; n = 16 cells).
source: This inhibition of spiking was more pronounced when iNC fibers were activated with a train of 4–5 light pulses at 50 Hz (pulse duration 10 ms), eliciting a longer spike delay (71 ± 44% increase; n = 16 cells, p < 0.05; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown by the current-clamp recordings in Figure 3F.

claim: In some recorded Golgi cells, trains of light pulses elicited a time locking of intrinsic spikes (n = 7) without clear inhibitory effect.
source: In some of the recorded Golgi cells, trains of light pulses elicited a time locking of intrinsic spikes (n = 7, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) without clear inhibitory effect, suggesting a network effect mediated through the gap junctions among Golgi cells (Dugué et al., 2009; Vervaeke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and interpreted based on known gap junction connectivity.

claim: The time locking of spikes suggests a network effect mediated through the gap junctions among Golgi cells.
source: In some of the recorded Golgi cells, trains of light pulses elicited a time locking of intrinsic spikes (n = 7, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) without clear inhibitory effect, suggesting a network effect mediated through the gap junctions among Golgi cells (Dugué et al., 2009; Vervaeke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and supported by citations.

claim: The iNC pathway inhibits spiking in Golgi cells.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that the iNC pathway inhibits spiking in Golgi cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the electrophysiological data in Figure 3.

claim: The rate of success in finding responsive Golgi cells was rather low (24% and 27% of all recorded Golgi cells in GlyT2-cre and GAD-cre mice, respectively).
source: The rate of success in finding responsive Golgi cells was rather low (24% and 27% of all recorded Golgi cells in GlyT2-cre and GAD-cre mice, respectively) suggesting that iNC axons might preferentially or exclusively inhibit a certain subpopulation of Golgi cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: iNC axons might preferentially or exclusively inhibit a certain subpopulation of Golgi cells.
source: The rate of success in finding responsive Golgi cells was rather low (24% and 27% of all recorded Golgi cells in GlyT2-cre and GAD-cre mice, respectively) suggesting that iNC axons might preferentially or exclusively inhibit a certain subpopulation of Golgi cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the low success rate of finding responsive cells.

claim: 64 out of 85 recorded Golgi cells fired spontaneously at low rates (mean frequency: 9.0 ± 6.5 Hz).
source: While analyzing our current-clamp recordings in GAD-cre mice, we noted considerable variability in Golgi cells' properties, with their spontaneous spiking showing the most striking difference (Figure 4A). While 64 out of 85 recorded Golgi cells fired spontaneously at low rates (mean frequency: 9.0 ± 6.5 Hz), the other 21 Golgi cells were quiescent and had a resting membrane potential negative to the spiking threshold (resting potential −55 ± 2.4 mV, spike threshold −43 ± 1 mV, n = 13 cells).
evidence: This is shown by the current-clamp recordings in Figure 4A.

claim: 21 out of 85 Golgi cells were quiescent and had a resting membrane potential negative to the spiking threshold (resting potential −55 ± 2.4 mV, spike threshold −43 ± 1 mV).
source: While analyzing our current-clamp recordings in GAD-cre mice, we noted considerable variability in Golgi cells' properties, with their spontaneous spiking showing the most striking difference (Figure 4A). While 64 out of 85 recorded Golgi cells fired spontaneously at low rates (mean frequency: 9.0 ± 6.5 Hz), the other 21 Golgi cells were quiescent and had a resting membrane potential negative to the spiking threshold (resting potential −55 ± 2.4 mV, spike threshold −43 ± 1 mV, n = 13 cells).
evidence: This is shown by the current-clamp recordings in Figure 4A.

claim: Only the spontaneously active Golgi cells were responsive to iNC stimulation.
source: When evaluating iNC effects in Golgi cells, it became obvious that only the spontaneously active Golgi cells ('s-Golgi cells') were responsive to iNC stimulation.
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 4A-B.

claim: 24 out of 64 (37.5%) spontaneously active Golgi cells were inhibited by iNC activation.
source: Specifically, 24 out of 64 (37.5%) s-Golgi cells were inhibited by iNC activation (Figure 4A–B; blue), whereas none of the 21 not-spontaneously spiking Golgi cells ('ns-Golgi cells'; green) were affected by the stimulation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: None of the 21 not-spontaneously spiking Golgi cells were affected by iNC stimulation.
source: Specifically, 24 out of 64 (37.5%) s-Golgi cells were inhibited by iNC activation (Figure 4A–B; blue), whereas none of the 21 not-spontaneously spiking Golgi cells ('ns-Golgi cells'; green) were affected by the stimulation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Repeating stimulations during depolarizing current injections that drove the ns-Golgi cells to continuous spiking also failed to reveal iNC effect.
source: Repeating these stimulations during depolarizing current injections that drove the ns-Golgi cells to continuous spiking also failed to reveal iNC effect (Figure 4A, top right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: iNC fibers inhibit preferentially spontaneously active Golgi cells.
source: These findings suggested that iNC fibers inhibit preferentially s-Golgi cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the electrophysiological data in Figure 4.

claim: The observed fraction of inhibited s-Golgi cells is bound to be underestimated because virus injections were unlikely to result in transfection of the entire iNC population.
source: It should be noted that our virus injections were unlikely to result in transfection of the entire iNC population, hence the observed fraction of inhibited s-Golgi cells is bound to be underestimated.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about the interpretation of the data.

claim: Spontaneously active Golgi cells differ from not-spontaneously spiking Golgi cells in action potential shape.
source: The s-Golgi cells differ from ns-Golgi cells also in action potential (AP) shape (Figure 4D) recorded during steady-state firing.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The AP waveform was shorter in s-Golgi cells compared to ns-Golgi cells.
source: The observation that the AP waveform (composed of AP and after-hyperpolarization [AHP]) was shorter in s-Golgi cells compared to ns-Golgi cells (Figure 4E; see Table 1) led us to seek for other distinguishing electrophysiological features.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and Table 1.

claim: ns-Golgi cells showed significantly larger variability in all of the AP shape measurements compared to s-Golgi cells.
source: Compared to the s-Golgi cells, the ns-Golgi cells showed significantly larger variability in all of the AP shape measurements, although no significant differences were found in their average values (see Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: No differences were found in population averages of the input–output relationship of the two Golgi cell groups.
source: Also, no differences were found in population averages of the input–output relationship of the two Golgi cell groups, as evidenced by nearly identical current-to-firing frequency (I-F) curves (Figure 4F; Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F and Table 1.

claim: ns- and s-Golgi cells did not differ as a population in their estimated capacitance (Cm), nor in their input resistance.
source: ns- and s-Golgi cells did not differ as a population in their estimated capacitance (Cm), nor in their input resistance, but analysis of their variance showed clear differences between the groups (Figure 4G, compare the significance values obtained with Wilcoxon and F-tests in Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G and Table 1.

claim: Analysis of variance showed clear differences between s-Golgi and ns-Golgi cells in capacitance and input resistance.
source: ns- and s-Golgi cells did not differ as a population in their estimated capacitance (Cm), nor in their input resistance, but analysis of their variance showed clear differences between the groups (Figure 4G, compare the significance values obtained with Wilcoxon and F-tests in Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G and Table 1.

claim: The s-Golgi cells accommodated very uniformly to roughly half of the initial firing frequency.
source: The population variability became most visible when comparing the steady-state frequency accommodation (Figure 4H, left, compare the significance values obtained with Wilcoxon and F-tests in Table 1): the s-Golgi cells accommodated very uniformly to roughly half of the initial firing frequency, while ns-Golgi cells showed either no adaptation (evidenced by steady-state accommodation values around 90% of control) or adapted even more than the s-Golgi cells (to 35% of control; compare the widths of blue and green bars in Figure 4H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4H.

claim: ns-Golgi cells showed either no adaptation or adapted even more than the s-Golgi cells.
source: The population variability became most visible when comparing the steady-state frequency accommodation (Figure 4H, left, compare the significance values obtained with Wilcoxon and F-tests in Table 1): the s-Golgi cells accommodated very uniformly to roughly half of the initial firing frequency, while ns-Golgi cells showed either no adaptation (evidenced by steady-state accommodation values around 90% of control) or adapted even more than the s-Golgi cells (to 35% of control; compare the widths of blue and green bars in Figure 4H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The large variability of ns-Golgi cells in frequency accommodation, AHP time, AP half width, Cm, input resistance, and AP shape suggest that the ns-Golgi cells form a heterogeneous group of cells consisting of several functionally distinct subpopulations.
source: The large variability of ns-Golgi cells in frequency accommodation, AHP time, AP half width, Cm, input resistance, and AP shape suggest that the ns-Golgi cells form a heterogeneous group of cells consisting of several functionally distinct subpopulations.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the variability analysis in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The majority of Golgi cells express the glycine transporter GlyT2, with most of them being of mixed GABA-glycinergic phenotype.
source: It is well established that Golgi cells are neurochemically heterogeneous (Ottersen et al., 1988; Simat et al., 2007; Pietrajtis and Dieudonné, 2013). While the majority of Golgi cells express the glycine transporter GlyT2, with most of them being of mixed GABA-glycinergic phenotype, about 15–20 % of Golgi cells are purely GABAergic (Ottersen et al., 1988; Simat et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous immunohistochemical studies.

claim: About 15–20% of Golgi cells are purely GABAergic.
source: It is well established that Golgi cells are neurochemically heterogeneous (Ottersen et al., 1988; Simat et al., 2007; Pietrajtis and Dieudonné, 2013). While the majority of Golgi cells express the glycine transporter GlyT2, with most of them being of mixed GABA-glycinergic phenotype, about 15–20 % of Golgi cells are purely GABAergic (Ottersen et al., 1988; Simat et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous immunohistochemical studies.

claim: GlyT2-expressing Golgi cells have previously been reported to be intrinsically silent.
source: GlyT2-expressing Golgi cells have previously been reported to be intrinsically silent (Dugué et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous electrophysiological study.

claim: The iNC-inhibited Golgi cells may correspond to the purely GABAergic Golgi cells.
source: We, thus, hypothesized that the iNC-inhibited Golgi cells, all of which fire spontaneously, may correspond to the purely GABAergic Golgi cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the electrophysiological and immunohistochemical evidence.

claim: All of the Golgi cells that express neurogranin are also GABAergic.
source: As all of the Golgi cells that express the calcium-binding protein, neurogranin are also GABAergic (Simat et al., 2007), we used neurogranin in conjunction with GlyT2-eGFP expression to differentiate pure GABAergic Golgi cells from the mixed GABA-glycinergic and pure glycinergic Golgi cell populations (Simat et al., 2007; Pietrajtis and Dieudonné, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous immunohistochemical study.

claim: iNC axons preferentially contact cell bodies and dendrites of Golgi cells that were intensely stained for neurogranin.
source: iNC axons were easily identified by their co-expression of eGFP and tdTomato and were found to preferentially contact cell bodies and dendrites of Golgi cells that were intensely stained for neurogranin (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is shown by the immunohistochemical images in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Selective targeting of neurogranin-positive cells by iNC fibers extended to the molecular layer.
source: This selective targeting of neurogranin-positive cells by iNC fibers extended to the ML (indicated by arrowheads in Figure 5C), as iNC fibers were seen to climb along the apical dendritic shafts of neurogranin-positive Golgi cells to the ML.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In GAD-cre animals, iNC fibers were found to impinge on the dendrites and cell bodies of Golgi cells strongly expressing neurogranin.
source: Similarly, in GAD-cre animals, iNC fibers transfected with YFP and co-stained for GAD65-67 were found to impinge on the dendrites and cell bodies of Golgi cells strongly expressing neurogranin (Figure 5D, arrowheads).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: K-means 2D clustering separated Golgi cells into two populations based on GlyT2-eGFP and neurogranin staining intensities.
source: The 2D distribution of the two staining intensities was separated into two populations based on k-means statistical clustering (Figure 5E; green population: n = 238 Golgi cells (75%); blue population: n = 79 Golgi cells (25%); see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Golgi cells in the two groups differed mainly in their eGFP staining, as illustrated by the bimodal distribution of the mean eGFP intensities.
source: Golgi cells in the two groups differed mainly in their eGFP staining, as illustrated by the bimodal distribution of the mean eGFP intensities (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The normalized neurogranin intensities were approximately 50% higher in the low-eGFP population.
source: The normalized neurogranin intensities were approximately 50% higher in the low-eGFP population (Wilcoxon test p < 0.00001), even though distributions overlapped extensively (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Most of the Golgi cells that were contacted by at least one iNC bouton were GABAergic Golgi cells (80%, n = 32 out of the 40 'iNC-contacted' cells).
source: Most of the Golgi cells that were contacted by at least one iNC bouton were GABAergic Golgi cells (80%, n = 32 out of the 40 'iNC-contacted' cells; Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H,I.

claim: Glycinergic Golgi cells were only rarely apposed to iNC boutons (3%, n = 8 out of 238 all Golgi cells; on average 1.88 ± 1.12 appositions per cell).
source: In contrast to the glycinergic Golgi cells that were only rarely apposed to iNC boutons (3%, n = 8 out of 238 all Golgi cells; on average 1.88 ± 1.12 appositions per cell; max = 4 appositions; 15 appositions found overall; Figure 5I, blue dots), 41% of the GABAergic Golgi cells were contacted by on average 7.65 ± 4.69 appositions (n = 32 out of 79 Golgi cells, max = 20 appositions; 245 appositions found overall; Figure 5I, blue dots).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I.

claim: 41% of the GABAergic Golgi cells were contacted by on average 7.65 ± 4.69 iNC appositions.
source: In contrast to the glycinergic Golgi cells that were only rarely apposed to iNC boutons (3%, n = 8 out of 238 all Golgi cells; on average 1.88 ± 1.12 appositions per cell; max = 4 appositions; 15 appositions found overall; Figure 5I, blue dots), 41% of the GABAergic Golgi cells were contacted by on average 7.65 ± 4.69 appositions (n = 32 out of 79 Golgi cells, max = 20 appositions; 245 appositions found overall; Figure 5I, blue dots).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I.

claim: iNC fibers contact almost exclusively the GABAergic Golgi cell population (97% of iNC terminals contact the GABAergic Golgi cell population).
source: These results demonstrate that iNC fibers contact almost exclusively the GABAergic Golgi cell population, as summarized in the schematic drawing of Figure 5J (97% of iNC terminals contact the GABAergic Golgi cell population).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5J and is a summary of the quantitative analysis.

claim: This is the first evidence for differential connectivity among subpopulations of Golgi cells.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first evidence for differential connectivity among subpopulations of Golgi cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: iNC neurons were silent in acute slices.
source: First, using acute slices from GlyT2-cre mice transfected as above, we performed extracellular recordings from iNC neurons, identified by their YFP fluorescence. iNC neurons were silent (n = 11 cells) in contrast with the other cell types in the CN (Uusisaari and Knöpfel, 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is shown by the extracellular recordings and supported by citations.

claim: Optogenetic excitation of iNC neurons by short light pulses (1 ms) evoked high-frequency bursts of spikes.
source: Optogenetic excitation of iNC neurons by short light pulses (1 ms) evoked high-frequency bursts of spikes (Figure 6A1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A1.

claim: Increasing the illumination power resulted in an increased number of spikes and in mean burst frequency, which saturated around 450 Hz for a light power of 1–2 mW/mm².
source: Increasing the illumination power resulted in an increased number of spikes and in mean burst frequency, which saturated around 450 Hz for a light power of 1–2 mW/mm² (Figure 6A2; n = 11 cells).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A2.

claim: At saturating illumination intensity (1.3 mW/mm2), stereotypical high-frequency bursts of spikes were evoked with short light durations (10 ms).
source: At saturating illumination intensity (1.3 mW/mm2), stereotypical high-frequency bursts of spikes were evoked with short light durations (10 ms), resembling the extracellular recordings in the GlyT2-cre slices.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B1.

claim: The bursts were riding on a depolarized plateau, which outlasted the illumination period, and were often followed by a prolonged depolarized after-potential and low-frequency firing.
source: These bursts were riding on a depolarized plateau, which outlasted the illumination period, and were often followed by a prolonged depolarized after-potential and low-frequency firing.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B1.

claim: Increasing the duration of the light pulse extended the burst duration without affecting the intra-burst frequency.
source: Increasing the duration of the light pulse extended the burst duration without affecting the intra-burst frequency (Figure 6B2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B2.

claim: High-frequency bursting of APs could constitute the main firing mode of iNC neurons in response to excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: These results indicate that high-frequency bursting of APs could constitute the main firing mode of iNC neurons in response to excitatory synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the optogenetic experiments in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Single 25-ms long light pulses suppressed spiking in 18 out of 86 recorded Golgi cells (21%) in vivo.
source: Based on our in vitro calibration (Figure 6A,B), single 25-ms long light pulses are expected to evoke short bursts of firing in the iNC neurons. This illumination protocol suppressed spiking in 18 out of 86 recorded Golgi cells (21%, Figure 6C2, left).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C2.

claim: 79% of Golgi cells and PNs did not show any significant modulation of the spiking frequency following illumination in vivo.
source: The rest of the Golgi cells (79%, Figure 6C2, middle) as well as PNs (n = 50 cells, Figure 6C2, right) did not show any significant modulation of the spiking frequency following illumination.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C2.

claim: The time course of the inhibition in the responsive Golgi cells was variable (duration: 23.4 ± 11.7 ms; onset latency: 14.5 ± 7.2 ms; peak latency: 25.4 ± 14.1 ms).
source: The time course of the inhibition in the responsive Golgi cells was variable (duration: 23.4 ± 11.7 ms; onset latency: 14.5 ± 7.2 ms; peak latency: 25.4 ± 14.1 ms; n = 18, Figure 6D2) as exemplified with colored traces from individual cells in Figure 6D1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D1,D2.

claim: Golgi cells' firing was robustly suppressed in vivo (frequency decreased to 1.58 ± 1.46 Hz from a baseline of 10.9 ± 3.9 Hz).
source: Regardless of this variability, Golgi cells' firing was robustly suppressed (frequency decreased to 1.58 ± 1.46 Hz from a baseline of 10.9 ± 3.9 Hz, n = 18 cells, Figure 6D3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D3.

claim: The average firing rate of responsive Golgi cells was significantly higher than the average FR of non-responsive Golgi cells (10.5 ± 3.5 Hz vs 8.2 ± 4.2 Hz).
source: Interestingly, the average firing rate (FR) of responsive Golgi cells was significantly higher than the average FR of non-responsive Golgi cells (10.5 ± 3.5 Hz, n = 18 cells vs 8.2 ± 4.2 Hz, n = 68 cells, respectively; Wilcoxon test: p = 0.036; Figure 6D4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D4.

claim: The results provide the first functional evidence for an iNC pathway suppressing GABAergic Golgi cell spiking.
source: Overall, our results provide the first functional evidence for an iNC pathway suppressing GABAergic Golgi cell spiking.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The iNC pathway likely modulates the inhibitory control of GrCs and thereby gating of sensori-motor inputs into the cerebellar cortex.
source: This pathway likely modulates the inhibitory control of GrCs and thereby gating of sensori-motor inputs into the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The iNC projection is formed by mixed GABA-glycinergic neurons of the CN and targets the GABAergic Golgi cells in the cerebellar cortex.
source: In the present work, we reveal an iNC pathway in the cerebellum. This projection is formed by mixed GABA-glycinergic neurons of the CN and targets the GABAergic Golgi cells in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The iNC axons originate from a population of mixed GABA-glycinergic CN neurons.
source: Here, using targeted viral transfection and labeling, we demonstrate that the iNC axons originate from a population of mixed GABA-glycinergic CN neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the anatomical findings.

claim: The iNC axon terminals were simple in their morphology, and rosette-like structures were never observed.
source: The iNC axon terminals were simple in their morphology, and rosette-like structures were never observed.
evidence: This is an anatomical observation from the confocal imaging.

claim: The GABAergic rosette-like terminals found in GrCL glomeruli must arise from extracerebellar sources.
source: Thus, the GABAergic rosette-like terminals found in GrCL glomeruli described in earlier works (Chan-Palay et al., 1979; Hámori and Takács, 1988) must arise from extracerebellar sources.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The morphology and spread of the iNC axons as well as the axonal bouton size was different from both the Golgi and Lugaro axons.
source: The morphology and spread of the iNC axons as well as the axonal bouton size was also different from both the Golgi and Lugaro axons (Dieudonné, 1998; Dumoulin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison with known axon types supported by citations.

claim: The study discards the suggestion that iNC axons would emerge as collaterals of GABAergic NO neurons.
source: Our study discards the suggestion that iNC axons would emerge as collaterals of GABAergic NO neurons (Figure 1; Tolbert et al., 1978; Haines, 1988).
evidence: This is based on the anatomical and size distribution analysis in Figure 1.

claim: The neurons transfected in the GlyT2-cre animals do not include NO cells.
source: The neurons transfected in the GlyT2-cre animals do not include NO cells, as evidenced by the lack of labeling in the IO (Husson et al., 2014; see also De Zeeuw et al., 1994) and the clear difference in cell body size between GlyT2-cre and NO neurons (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is shown by the lack of IO labeling and size distribution analysis in Figure 1.

claim: All the fibers found in the cortex in GAD-cre mice were GlyT2 immunopositive, demonstrating that only those GABAergic CN cells that also express GlyT2 project to the cortex.
source: While viral transfection protocols used in the GAD-cre mice also transfect NO cells (Lefler et al., 2014; Figure 1A3), all the fibers found in the cortex were GlyT2 immunopositive, demonstrating that only those GABAergic CN cells that also express GlyT2 project to the cortex.
evidence: This is shown by the immunohistochemical analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: The purely glycinergic neurons of the medial CN nucleus projecting to the vestibular nuclei are unlikely to be the source of the iNC axons.
source: Also, as the purely glycinergic neurons of the medial CN nucleus projecting to the vestibular nuclei (Bagnall et al., 2009) are not found in the main targets of viral transfections in the present study (interpositus and lateral CN), they are unlikely to be the source of the iNC axons.
evidence: This is based on the anatomical location of the transfections and supported by citation.

claim: iNC fibers undoubtedly represent the axons of a single mixed CN neuron type.
source: The nucleo-cortical axons in both GlyT2-cre and GAD-cre models were very similar in shape and function and co-stained for GAD and GlyT2, respectively (Figure 2). The small differences observed are likely to originate from variability in fixation procedures and wavelength dependence of optical resolution. Therefore, iNC fibers undoubtedly represent the axons of a single mixed CN neuron type.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the anatomical and immunohistochemical data in Figure 2.

claim: The density of nucleo-cortical fibers in the GAD-cre model was somewhat higher than in the GlyT2-cre model.
source: The density of nucleo-cortical fibers in the GAD-cre model was somewhat higher than in the GlyT2-cre model (compare panels 2A1 and 2B1), most likely due to the mosaic expression of cre in only 50% of mixed neurons in the GlyT2-cre mice (Husson et al., 2014) as well as the stronger expression levels obtained with the AAV9 serotype virus used in the GAD-cre model.
evidence: This is an observation from the confocal images and explained by methodological factors.

claim: The iNC neurons show morphological and electrophysiological resemblances to the CN glycinergic neurons described in recent studies as spontaneously inactive, mixed GABA-glycinergic neurons.
source: The iNC neurons described in the present work show clear morphological (Figure 1B2) and electrophysiological (Figure 6) resemblances to the CN glycinergic neurons described in two recent studies as spontaneously inactive, mixed GABA-glycinergic neurons (compare the present results with Figure 1 in Uusisaari and Knöpfel, 2010 and Figure 7Ab in Husson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: The iNC neurons, the 'Gly-I' neurons, and the mixed GABA-glycinergic neurons are the same cells.
source: Thus, we conclude that the iNC neurons, the 'Gly-I' neurons, and the mixed GABA-glycinergic neurons are the same cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: The projection to the cortex is the most distinguishing feature of iNC neurons.
source: While these neurons also have local axon collaterals within in the CN (Husson et al., 2014), their projection to the cortex is their most distinguishing feature.
evidence: This is based on the anatomical findings and comparison with previous work.

claim: The authors propose that these neurons should be referred to as 'iNC' neurons.
source: Thus, we propose that they should be referred to as 'iNC' neurons.
evidence: This is a nomenclature proposal based on the findings.

claim: Golgi cells have previously been shown to receive inhibitory synapses from both Lugaro and other Golgi cells in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Golgi cells have previously been shown to receive inhibitory synapses from both Lugaro and other Golgi cells in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about known connectivity in the cerebellar cortex.

claim: Single iNC projection axons form numerous terminal swellings on the somata and dendrites of Golgi cells.
source: We demonstrate here that single iNC projection axons form numerous terminal swellings on the somata and dendrites of Golgi cells (Figure 2), somewhat reminiscent of the climbing fiber articulation on Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2.

claim: The average synaptic conductance at the iNC synapses is about six times the conductance reported at unitary Golgi–Golgi synapses.
source: The average synaptic conductance at the iNC synapses (estimated to be 1.9 and 8.5 nS in physiological and symmetrical chloride, respectively) is about six times the conductance reported at unitary Golgi–Golgi synapses (0.33 nS in physiological chloride; Hull and Regehr, 2011) and similar to the conductance at Lugaro to Golgi cell synapses in the juvenile animal (Dumoulin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous measurements supported by citations.

claim: The spatially restricted light stimulation likely activated a single or only a few iNC axons.
source: As our spatially restricted light stimulation likely activated a single or only a few iNC axons, the evoked IPSCs likely represent unitary responses through the multiple contacts made by single axons on Golgi cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental conditions.

claim: The evoked IPSCs likely represent unitary responses through the multiple contacts made by single axons on Golgi cells.
source: As our spatially restricted light stimulation likely activated a single or only a few iNC axons, the evoked IPSCs likely represent unitary responses through the multiple contacts made by single axons on Golgi cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental conditions and anatomical findings.

claim: Most of the current physiological work on Golgi cells tends to assume a homogeneous neuronal population.
source: Most of the current physiological work on Golgi cells tends to assume a homogeneous neuronal population while simultaneously using various, partly contradictory, identification criteria to target them for experiments (Schulman and Bloom, 1981; Holtzman et al., 2006; Xu and Edgley, 2008; Hull and Regehr, 2011; Hull et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: Accumulating evidence indicates that Golgi cells can be divided into different groups based on their neurotransmitter content and specific molecular marker expression.
source: However, accumulating evidence indicates that Golgi cells can be divided into different groups based on their neurotransmitter content (GABA, glycine or both; Ottersen et al., 1988) as well as specific molecular marker expression (Simat et al., 2007; Dugué et al., 2009; Pietrajtis and Dieudonné, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study presents the first evidence that neurochemical subtypes of Golgi cells may participate in specific microcircuits.
source: By demonstrating that the Golgi cells contacted by the iNC axons are characterized by none or low level of GlyT2-eGFP staining as well as high-neurogranin expression (Figure 5; compare with 'type 4' Golgi cells in Simat et al., 2007), we present the first evidence that neurochemical subtypes of Golgi cells may participate in specific microcircuits.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: The work supports the functional specialization of purely GABAergic Golgi cells by showing that they can be distinguished from other Golgi cells based on their electrophysiological properties.
source: Our work further supports the functional specialization of purely GABAergic Golgi cells by showing that they can be distinguished from other Golgi cells based on their electrophysiological properties (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the electrophysiological characterization in Figure 4.

source: Thus, while further work elucidating the functional role of the eNC projection to the cerebellar GrC layer is sorely needed, we conclude here that the inhibition of Golgi cell spiking observed in vivo (Figure 6) is mainly caused by a direct inhibition by the iNC axon terminals impinging on Golgi cell dendrites and cell bodies.

source: While there is no direct evidence either for or against any of these sources, a few earlier works have described inhibition of Golgi cells in response to electrical stimulation of the IO or to sensory stimulation (Schulman and Bloom, 1981; Xu and Edgley, 2008), suggesting that the IO might be the source of excitatory drive for iNC neurons.
